mainTopic: Is the dispute about vowing with בשר בכור the same as the question of whether a person means the animal before or after זריקת דמים? The גמרא says no: the dispute is really about whether a נדר can take hold through something forbidden by the Torah (דבר האסור) rather than by a vow (דבר הנדור).
overview: The amud opens by asking whether the dispute about someone who compares his meat to בשר בכור depends on which stage of the animal he means, before or after זריקת דמים. The גמרא answers no: everyone agrees he means the stage before the sprinkling. The real argument is whether a vow can be attached to a דבר האסור, something the Torah forbids, or only to a דבר הנדור, something forbidden through a vow. The one who permits learns from 'כי ידר' that only a דבר הנדור works, and uses 'לה׳' to include חטאת and אשם, which a person makes holy by declaring them. The one who forbids points to a ברייתא in the name of רבי that there is a מצוה to declare a בכור holy. The other side answers that a בכור is holy even without that declaration. Next, a ברייתא lists Temple items like the lamb, the pens, the altar and ירושלים, and the גמרא identifies it as רבי מאיר. It then reconciles the ברייתא's second half with his view by splitting 'not for a lamb' from 'for a lamb'. A new משנה follows about vows that use the names of offerings. The גמרא says its unattributed author is רבי מאיר, then challenges this from a ברייתא that permits 'הא קרבן', which only swears by the life of an offering. The answer to that challenge comes on the next amud.

steps.title: Is the firstborn-meat dispute a disagreement between תנאים about the animal's stage?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא describes the case: a person puts בשר בכור next to other meat and says 'this is like this.' It then asks whether the dispute over this case is really an argument between תנאים about which stage of the בכור he is referring to.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where he places meat of a בכור, places other meat next to it, and says 'this is like this.' Is it then a dispute between תנאים?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its description of the case and suggesting a possible reading of the dispute. This sets up the next step, where the suggestion will be tested.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before its blood is sprinkled, a בכור is holy and forbidden. After the sprinkling, its meat may be eaten by כהנים. The גמרא suggests that the two sides argue about which of those stages the person meant when he compared his meat to the בכור.

keyTerms.meaning: meat of a firstborn animal, which is holy
he places or puts down
'this is like this', the words that attach a vow to something else
it is a dispute between תנאים

phrases.english: where he places meat of a firstborn animal
and places other meat next to it,
and he said: 'This is like this.'
And is it a dispute between תנאים?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion on the daf about vowing with holy meat.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the dispute about 'like בשר בכור' depends on which stage of the animal the person meant.

steps.title: No: everyone means before the sprinkling, and the one who permits learns from 'כי ידר'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggestion. Everyone agrees the person means the stage before זריקת דמים. The one who permits has a reason from the פסוק: a vow must be attached to a דבר הנדור, and a בכור is a דבר האסור.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees he means before the sprinkling of the blood. The one who permits relies on the פסוק 'כי ידר': the vow must be made with an item that became forbidden through a vow. That leaves out a בכור, which is forbidden on its own by the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says 'no' to the suggestion and gives the real reason behind the side that permits.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument moves away from 'which stage did he mean' to 'what kind of item can a vow be attached to.' A בכור is holy from birth, so nobody's vow made it forbidden. Because of that, according to this view, you cannot attach a vow to it.

keyTerms.meaning: everyone agrees
sprinkling of the blood on the מזבח
an item that became forbidden through a vow
an item that the Torah itself forbids
to exclude

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up דבר הנדור with דבר האסור. The first became forbidden because a person vowed. The second is forbidden by the Torah with no vow involved, like a בכור.

phrases.aramaic: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לִפְנֵי זְרִיקַת דָּמִים,
phrases.english: No, everyone agrees he means before the sprinkling of the blood,
and what is the reason of the one who permits?
The verse says: 'When he vows,'
meaning it is not a vow until he vows with an item forbidden through a vow,
which excludes a firstborn, since it is an item forbidden by the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion from step 1 and replaces it with a source-based explanation.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the dispute is about which stage of the בכור the person meant.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Both sides agree he means before the sprinkling. The argument is really about whether a דבר האסור can carry a vow.
steps.whyThisMatters: It introduces the key idea that a vow takes hold through a דבר הנדור, a rule that comes up throughout נדרים.

steps.title: The one who forbids learns from 'לה׳' that a דבר האסור also works
steps.stepSummary: The side that forbids learns from the word 'לה׳' that a vow can be attached even to something the Torah forbids.
steps.simpleTranslation: The one who forbids relies on the פסוק 'to the Lord,' which comes to include an item forbidden by the Torah.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the reason for the other side, the one who forbids.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This side reads the extra word 'לה׳' as widening the rule. Anything that belongs to ה׳, even if no vow made it holy, can serve as the item a vow is attached to.

keyTerms.meaning: 'to ה׳', the word in the פסוק
to include

phrases.english: And the one who forbids: the verse says 'to the Lord,'
to include an item forbidden by the Torah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the explanation by giving the source for the opposing side.
steps.raayaObject: The view in step 2 that forbids: a vow attached to a דבר האסור also takes effect.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The word 'לה׳' includes a vow attached to a דבר האסור such as a בכור.

steps.title: What does the one who permits do with 'לה׳'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the side that permits explains the word 'לה׳', since it does not use the word to include a דבר האסור.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the one who permits: what does he do with 'to the Lord'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the extra word means for the side that permits. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes every word in the Torah teaches something. If the one who permits does not use 'לה׳' to include a דבר האסור, he must use it for something else.

keyTerms.meaning: what does he do with it, meaning how does he explain it

phrases.english: And the one who permits, what does he do with 'to the Lord'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the side that permits about the source used by the side that forbids.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the one who permits learns from the word 'לה׳'.

steps.title: He uses 'לה׳' for attaching a vow to a חטאת or אשם
steps.stepSummary: The one who permits uses 'לה׳' to include a person who attaches his vow to a חטאת or an אשם.
steps.simpleTranslation: He needs it to include someone who attaches his vow to a sin-offering or a guilt-offering.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the one who permits uses 'לה׳' to include a vow attached to a חטאת or an אשם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A חטאת or אשם becomes holy when the person sets the animal aside, so it is somewhat like a vowed item. However, he is obligated to bring it, so without the extra word one might think it does not count. 'לה׳' teaches that it does count, while a בכור, which is holy on its own, still does not.

keyTerms.meaning: he needs it for
one who attaches his vow to another item
sin-offering and guilt-offering

steps.whatToRemember: Everyone agrees the person means the בכור before זריקת דמים. The argument is whether a vow can be attached to a דבר האסור. The one who permits learns from 'כי ידר' that only a דבר הנדור works, and uses 'לה׳' for חטאת and אשם. The one who forbids uses 'לה׳' to include a דבר האסור.

phrases.english: He needs it for one who attaches his vow to a sin-offering or a guilt-offering.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'לה׳' teaches that a vow attached to a חטאת or אשם takes effect.

steps.title: Why include חטאת and אשם but leave out the בכור?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks the one who permits what reason he has for using 'לה׳' to include חטאת and אשם while leaving out the בכור.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what made you decide to include a חטאת and an אשם, and to leave out the בכור?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 5. It asks why 'לה׳' covers חטאת and אשם but not a בכור, since all three are holy animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 5, the one who permits used 'לה׳' to include a vow attached to a חטאת or אשם. A בכור is also a holy קרבן, so the גמרא wants to know what makes it different.

keyTerms.meaning: What did you see? This asks for the reason behind a choice between two options.
To include something in a law, based on a word in the פסוק
To leave something out of a law

phrases.english: And what did you see to include
a sin-offering and a guilt-offering
and to exclude the firstborn?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמָה רָאִיתָ לְרַבּוֹת חַטָּאת וְאָשָׁם וּלְהוֹצִיא אֶת הַבְּכוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the reasoning behind the answer in step 5
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What difference between חטאת/אשם and בכור justifies including the first two and leaving out the בכור?

steps.title: חטאת and אשם are holy through a vow, but a בכור is holy from birth
steps.stepSummary: חטאת and אשם become holy because a person declares them, which makes them 'vow-made.' A בכור is holy from its mother's womb.
steps.simpleTranslation: I include חטאת and אשם because with them a person is attaching his vow to something made holy by a vow. I leave out the בכור because it is holy from its mother's womb.
steps.whatsHappening: The one who permits explains the difference. A person makes a חטאת or אשם holy by declaring it, but a בכור is holy on its own from birth.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A vow can only be attached to something that became forbidden through a vow (a דבר הנדור). A חטאת or אשם fits this, because a person's declaration made it holy. A בכור never needed anyone's declaration, so it counts as forbidden by the Torah itself (a דבר האסור).

keyTerms.meaning: Attaching a vow to something that became forbidden through a vow
Holy from its mother's womb, meaning holy automatically from birth

phrases.english: I include a sin-offering and a guilt-offering
because he attaches it to something forbidden by a vow,
phrases.notes: A person chooses an animal and declares it a חטאת or אשם, so its holiness comes from his own words.

phrases.english: and I exclude the firstborn
because it is holy from its mother's womb.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: חטאת and אשם are holy through a person's declaration (נדר), while a בכור is holy automatically from birth

steps.title: The one who forbids: a בכור also counts as holy through a vow
steps.stepSummary: The one who forbids holds that attaching a vow to a בכור also counts as attaching it to something holy through a vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the one who forbids holds that a בכור is also attaching to something made holy by a vow.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now explains the other side. The one who forbids says that a בכור also has a vow element. The proof comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This attacks the distinction made in step 7. If a בכור also counts as a דבר הנדור, then a vow can be attached to it like any other קרבן, and the vow takes effect.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who forbids (here, the one who says the vow takes effect)
Also

phrases.english: And the one who forbids,
a firstborn too is something one attaches to as a vow item.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאן דְּאָסַר בְּכוֹר נָמֵי מַתְפִּיסוֹ בְּנֶדֶר הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing view to the distinction in step 7
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the one who forbids, a בכור also counts as a דבר הנדור

steps.title: Proof from רבי: there is a מצוה to declare a בכור holy
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא in the name of רבי teaches that there is a מצוה to declare a בכור born in one's home holy, from the פסוק 'הַזָּכָר תַּקְדִּישׁ'.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches, they said in the name of רבי: From where do we know that when a בכור is born in a person's home, there is a מצוה to declare it holy? Because it says, 'The male you shall make holy.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to support the one who forbids. The owner of a בכור is commanded to declare it holy out loud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Torah wants the owner to declare the בכור holy, then the בכור has a vow element too, just like a חטאת or אשם. This weakens the claim that a בכור is only a דבר האסור.

keyTerms.meaning: To declare it holy
'The male you shall make holy,' the פסוק about a בכור

phrases.english: As it is taught: they said in the name of Rabbi:
From where do we know, for one who has a firstborn born in his home,
that it is a מצוה to consecrate it,
as it is stated: "The male you shall consecrate."

steps.raayaObject: That a בכור also counts as a דבר הנדור
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא in the name of רבי, from 'הַזָּכָר תַּקְדִּישׁ' (דברים 15:19)

steps.title: The one who permits: a בכור is holy even without the declaration
steps.stepSummary: The one who permits answers that even if the owner does not declare the בכור holy, it is still holy. So its holiness does not come from a vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the one who permits says: if he does not declare it holy, is it not holy anyway?
steps.whatsHappening: The one who permits pushes back against the proof from רבי. The declaration is only a מצוה, and the בכור is holy either way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מצוה to declare it holy does not create the holiness, because the בכור is already holy from birth. So the בכור is still a דבר האסור, forbidden by the Torah, and a vow attached to it does not take effect.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who permits (here, the one who says the vow does not take effect)
Does it not become holy? This is a rhetorical question meaning 'of course it is holy.'

steps.whatToRemember: Both sides agree that there is a מצוה to declare a בכור holy. They argue only about whether that declaration makes it a 'vow-made' item. The one who permits says no, because the בכור is holy even without it.

phrases.english: And the one who permits,
when he does not consecrate it,
is it not consecrated?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאן דְּשָׁרֵי כִּי לָא מַקְדֵּישׁ לֵיהּ מִי לָא מִיקַּדֵּישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the proof of step 9 from the permitting side
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the idea that the מצוה to declare a בכור holy turns it into a דבר הנדור
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The holiness of a בכור does not depend on the declaration, since it is holy even without one

steps.title: Quoting the next words of the משנה: like the lamb, like the enclosures
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next words of the משנה, 'כְּאִימְּרָא' and 'כַּדִּירִים', to begin discussing them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new section. It quotes the next phrases of the משנה to set up the discussion that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These are more ways of attaching a vow to a קרבן: 'like the lamb' (the daily offering) and 'like the enclosures' (animals set aside as קרבנות). The explanation comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: Like the lamb, meaning the lamb of the daily offering (תמיד)
Like the enclosures, meaning animals kept in pens as קרבנות

phrases.english: "Like the lamb," "like the enclosures."
phrases.notes: These are words quoted from our משנה, which says a vow like this takes effect.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic by quoting the next phrase of the משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Quotes the next phrases of the משנה to set up the discussion that follows

steps.title: A ברייתא lists vow phrases using Temple items
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists seven holy Temple items, each said three ways. With 'that which I eat of yours' the food is forbidden; with 'that which I will not eat of yours' it is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught: 'A lamb, for a lamb, like a lamb; pens, for pens, like pens; wood, for wood, like wood; fires, for fires, like fires; altar, for the altar, like the altar; היכל, for the היכל, like the היכל; ירושלים, for ירושלים, like ירושלים.' In all of them, if he says 'that which I eat of yours', it is forbidden. If he says 'that which I will not eat of yours', it is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that explains the משנה's words 'כאימרא' and 'כדירים'. It adds a full list of Temple items and three ways of saying each one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each item is holy, so tying food to it makes a vow that forbids the food. The ברייתא treats the plain form, the 'for' form and the 'like' form the same. What decides the case is the ending: 'that I eat' forbids the food, and 'that I will not eat' leaves it permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Lamb, here the lamb of the daily offering (תמיד)
Pens or enclosures for animals set aside as offerings
The fires of the altar
The Sanctuary building in the בית המקדש

steps.confusionAlert: The three forms (plain, 'for', 'like') are not three different rulings. In this ברייתא they all work the same way. Only the ending, 'I eat' or 'I will not eat', changes the result.

phrases.english: It was taught: 'A lamb,' 'for a lamb,' 'like a lamb,'
'pens,' 'for pens,' 'like pens,'
'wood,' 'for wood,' 'like wood,'
phrases.notes: This means the wood set aside to burn on the altar.

phrases.english: 'fires,' 'for fires,' 'like fires,'
'altar,' 'for the altar,' 'like the altar,'
'Sanctuary,' 'for the Sanctuary,' 'like the Sanctuary,'
'Jerusalem,' 'for Jerusalem,' 'like Jerusalem,'
In all of them, if he adds 'that which I eat of yours,' it is forbidden.
If he adds 'that which I will not eat of yours,' it is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the משנה words that were quoted in step 11.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Using any of the listed Temple items in any of the three forms makes a vow if he says 'that I eat'. If he says 'that I will not eat', the food stays permitted.

steps.title: Identifying the ברייתא as רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא identifies the ברייתא's author as רבי מאיר, because he treats 'lamb', 'for a lamb' and 'like a lamb' the same.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whom have we heard say there is no difference between 'lamb', 'for a lamb' and 'like a lamb'? It is רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which תנא wrote this ברייתא and answers right away: רבי מאיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא makes all three forms work as a vow. That matches רבי מאיר, who does not draw a line between them. רבי יהודה holds only 'like a lamb' works. Naming רבי מאיר as the author sets up the challenge in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Whom have we heard (who is known to hold this view)?
There is no difference for him

phrases.english: Whom have we heard
who holds there is no difference
between 'a lamb,' 'for a lamb,' and 'like a lamb'?
It is Rabbi Meir.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Identifies the author of the ברייתא from step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first half of the ברייתא follows רבי מאיר.

steps.title: The second half seems to clash with רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא's second half permits 'I will not eat of yours'. But in a משנה רבי מאיר forbids 'לקרבן I will not eat of yours', and רבי אבא explains that as 'let it be for an offering, so I will not eat'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now look at the end: in all of them, 'that which I will not eat of yours' is permitted. But we learned in a משנה: 'לקרבן, that which I will not eat of yours', and רבי מאיר forbids it. רבי אבא said: it is as if he said, 'Let it be for an offering, and therefore I will not eat of yours.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the claim that the whole ברייתא is רבי מאיר. A משנה shows רבי מאיר forbids the food even when the person says 'I will not eat'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבא reads 'לקרבן לא אוכל לך' as two parts: 'for an offering', meaning the food is holy, and then 'so I will not eat it'. Since 'לאימרא' has the same 'for' form as 'לקרבן', רבי מאיר should forbid 'לאימרא לא אוכל לך' too. Yet the ברייתא permits it.

keyTerms.meaning: Say the end part (look at the latter clause)
For an offering
Therefore

phrases.english: Say the latter clause:
'And in all of them, "that which I will not eat of yours" is permitted.'
But didn't we learn: 'For an offering, that which I will not eat of yours'
Rabbi Meir forbids it,
phrases.notes: This is the very next משנה, which we will see in full in step 16.

phrases.english: and Rabbi Abba said:
It is as if he said, 'Let it be for an offering,
and therefore I will not eat of yours.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the identification made in step 13 by checking the ברייתא's second half.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא, including its permissive end, follows רבי מאיר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the משנה רבי מאיר forbids 'for an offering, I will not eat', because רבי אבא reads it as 'it is an offering, so I won't eat'. The same reading should forbid 'for a lamb, I will not eat', but the ברייתא permits it.

steps.title: Different wordings: 'not for a lamb' versus 'for a lamb'
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is about someone who said 'not for a lamb', and the משנה is about someone who said 'for a lamb'.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not difficult. This one (the ברייתא) is where he said 'לא לאימרא', 'not for a lamb'. That one (the משנה) is where he said 'לאימרא', 'for a lamb'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the clash by showing that the two sources are talking about different wordings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When he says 'for a lamb, I will not eat', he first declares the food holy and then refuses it, so רבי מאיר forbids it. When he says 'what I do not eat shall not be for a lamb', he only says something about food he does not eat. It might hint that food he eats is like the lamb, but רבי מאיר does not build a vow from what is only hinted by a negative statement, so the food is permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult (the question can be answered)
This one ... that one (pointing to two different cases)
Not for a lamb

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא does follow רבי מאיר. 'For a lamb, I will not eat' is forbidden, because he declares the food holy and then refuses it. 'Not for a lamb' is permitted, because he never directly declares anything holy.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
This is where he said 'not for a lamb,'
phrases.notes: 'This' is the ברייתא, which permits the food.

phrases.english: that is where he said 'for a lamb.'
phrases.notes: 'That' is the case that works like the משנה's 'לקרבן', which רבי מאיר forbids.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's permitted case and the משנה's forbidden case both involve 'for X, I will not eat', so they contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about 'not for a lamb', which is permitted. The משנה is about 'for a lamb' or 'for an offering', which רבי מאיר forbids. There is no contradiction, and the ברייתא follows רבי מאיר.

steps.title: The משנה on vows using offering names
steps.stepSummary: Saying 'an offering', 'a burnt-offering' and the like, followed by 'that which I eat of yours', makes the food forbidden, but רבי יהודה permits it. 'The offering', 'like an offering' and 'an offering, that which I will eat of yours' are forbidden. 'For an offering, I will not eat of yours' is forbidden according to רבי מאיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a person says 'קרבן', 'עולה', 'מנחה', 'חטאת', 'תודה' or 'שלמים', and adds 'that which I eat of yours', the food is forbidden. רבי יהודה permits it. If he says 'הקרבן', 'כקרבן', or 'קרבן, that which I will eat of yours', it is forbidden. If he says 'לקרבן, I will not eat of yours', רבי מאיר forbids it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lists different ways a person might use the names of Temple offerings to make his friend's food forbidden to himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each wording is a little different: a bare name (קרבן), 'the' (הקרבן), 'like' (כקרבן), and 'for' (לקרבן). In the first group the תנא קמא forbids the food, while רבי יהודה permits it. The last case, with a negative ('I will not eat'), is attributed by name to רבי מאיר.

keyTerms.meaning: An offering brought in the בית המקדש. Here it is used as a vow word to make food forbidden.
'The offering'. The word starts with ה, 'the'.
'Like an offering'. The word starts with כ, 'like'.
'For an offering' or 'let it be an offering'. The word starts with ל, 'for'.
Permits. Here it means the vow does not take effect.

steps.confusionAlert: Watch the little prefix letters: ה (the), כ (like) and ל (for). The whole sugya turns on whether these small letters change the meaning of the vow.

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who says: 'An offering', 'a burnt-offering', 'a meal-offering',
'a sin-offering', 'a thanks-offering', 'a peace-offering',
'that which I eat of yours': it is forbidden.
רבי יהודה permits it.
'The offering', 'like an offering', 'an offering, that which I will eat of yours': it is forbidden.

phrases.aramaic: ״לַקׇּרְבָּן לֹא אוֹכַל לָךְ״ — רַבִּי מֵאִיר אוֹסֵר.
phrases.english: 'For an offering, I will not eat of yours': רבי מאיר forbids it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new משנה opens a new discussion after the earlier ברייתא sugya.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Offering names followed by 'that which I eat of yours' make the food forbidden (רבי יהודה permits). הקרבן, כקרבן and קרבן are forbidden. In the case of לקרבן with 'I will not eat', רבי מאיר forbids.

steps.title: The unattributed משנה follows רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: Since the משנה forbids 'an offering', 'the offering' and 'like an offering' alike, its unattributed author must be רבי מאיר. He sees no difference between 'a lamb' and 'for a lamb'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה teaches that 'קרבן', 'הקרבן' and 'כקרבן, that which I will eat of yours' are all forbidden. So the unattributed part was taught like רבי מאיר, for whom 'a lamb' and 'for a lamb' are the same.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא figures out who wrote the unattributed (סתם) part of the משנה. It says it is רבי מאיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gives a bare 'offering' and 'like an offering' the same ruling. Earlier (step 13) we learned that רבי מאיר is the one who treats a bare word and a word with a prefix the same. So this סתם משנה matches his view.

keyTerms.meaning: An unattributed statement, one that does not name a רבי.
It makes no difference to him.

phrases.english: GEMARA: It teaches: 'An offering', 'the offering',
'like an offering, that which I will eat of yours': it is forbidden.
The unattributed opinion was taught according to רבי מאיר,
for whom there is no difference
between 'a lamb' and 'for a lamb'.
phrases.notes: This points back to רבי מאיר's view from step 13, where 'lamb' and 'for a lamb' were treated the same.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Identifies the author of the unattributed part of the משנה in step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The סתם משנה follows רבי מאיר, who makes no difference between a bare word and the same word with a prefix.

steps.title: But even the חכמים permit 'this offering'
steps.stepSummary: If the משנה follows רבי מאיר, why does it forbid 'the offering'? A ברייתא says the חכמים agree with רבי יהודה that 'this offering, that I will eat of yours' is permitted, since it is only swearing by the life of an offering.
steps.simpleTranslation: If this is רבי מאיר, look at what the משנה teaches: 'the offering, that which I will eat of yours' is forbidden. But a ברייתא teaches that the חכמים agree with רבי יהודה that one who says 'this offering', 'this burnt-offering', 'this meal-offering' or 'this sin-offering, that I will eat of yours' is permitted. That is because he did not make a vow; he only swore by the life of an offering!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges what it just said. It points out a ברייתא that seems to clash with the משנה's ruling on 'הקרבן'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'הקרבן' (the offering) sounds just like 'הא קרבן' (this offering). The ברייתא says even the חכמים, which includes רבי מאיר, agree that 'הא קרבן' is permitted, because it means 'by the life of the offering', and that is not a vow word. So how can a משנה that follows רבי מאיר forbid 'הקרבן'?

keyTerms.meaning: The חכמים agree, even though they usually argue.
'This offering'. It sounds almost the same as הַקָּרְבָּן.
By the life of an offering. This is like an oath, not a vow that ties the food to an offering.

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up הַקָּרְבָּן ('the offering', one word) and הָא קָרְבָּן ('this offering', two words). They sound almost the same, and that is the whole point of the challenge.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the exact wording of a vow decides whether it takes effect at all. Swearing 'by the life of' something is a different kind of statement from making food like an offering.

but isn't it taught: The חכמים agree with רבי יהודה
about one who says 'this offering', or 'this burnt-offering',

that it is permitted?
Because this person did not make a vow
except by the life of an offering!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 17's claim that the סתם משנה follows רבי מאיר.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the משנה, which forbids 'הקרבן שאוכל לך', follows רבי מאיר.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא says even the חכמים, including רבי מאיר, permit 'הא קרבן', which sounds the same as 'הקרבן', because it is only swearing by the life of an offering. So a משנה that follows רבי מאיר should not forbid 'הקרבן'.
